items.title: The middle income trap is real but not universal
items.claim: Many countries that reached middle income status (typically $4,000-$12,000 GDP per capita) have struggled to advance to high income. Which describes the phenomenon best?

options.text: A subset (Brazil, South Africa, Argentina, Thailand) have plateaued; others (South Korea, Singapore, Taiwan, more recently Poland) have transitioned successfully. Drivers include education, institutional quality, R&D, and shifting from labour-intensive to knowledge-intensive production
All countries reach high income automatically

items.reveal:
The term was popularised by Indermit Gill and Homi Kharas's 2007 World Bank study. World Bank research (2013, 2018) found about 13 of 101 middle-income economies in 1960 reached high income by 2008.

South Korea's transition from low- to high-income was unusually rapid (1960-2000). It combined export orientation, investment in education and selective industrial policy. Argentina's reversal (from rich to middle income across the 20th century) shows the direction isn't fixed.
items.why: Development outcomes are heterogeneous. Single-factor explanations (geography, institutions, culture) often capture parts of the story but don't generalise.

items.title: Quantitative easing is not 'printing money'
items.claim: Central banks engaged in QE after 2008 and again in 2020-21. Which describes the operation most accurately?

options.text: Central banks printed physical banknotes and gave them to households
Central banks created reserves electronically and used them to buy government bonds (and other assets) from financial institutions; reserves are central bank liabilities, not currency in circulation
QE doubled the M2 money supply directly

items.reveal:
By 2022, the Bank of England's gilt holdings under QE reached £895bn; the Fed's balance sheet peaked near $9 trillion. The reserves created are held by banks at the central bank; they don't enter the real economy as cash.

The mechanism is meant to lower long-term interest rates, support asset prices and ease financial conditions. Whether QE caused 2021-22 inflation is debated; the consensus is the energy shock and pandemic supply disruptions were the dominant drivers, with QE perhaps contributing at the margin.
items.why: 'Printing money' is a misleading shorthand for QE that conflates electronic reserve creation with currency issuance. The mechanisms have different implications.
